lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 4 you met how texts are built. Which structure tells events in the order they happened? Time order (also called chronological order).
Two texts about the same topic can be built in different ways. One might tell events in time order; another might explain causes and effects.
Example: Text A tells the steps of the first Moon landing in 1969, in order. Text B explains why the landing was possible: better rockets and computers.
Two accounts of the same event can differ too. A firsthand account is written by someone who was there, using I and we. A secondhand account is written by someone who read or heard about it.
A firsthand account shows feelings and close details. A secondhand account often gives more facts and the bigger picture.

Try it in the world: after an adventure with a friend in the game, each write it down: yours a firsthand account, then a secondhand one of what your friend saw. Compare them. Next: many sources, one answer.

exercises.prompt: Who writes a firsthand account?
exercises.explain: A firsthand account comes from someone who was there.

exercises.prompt: A diary written during a flood is a firsthand account.
exercises.explain: Yes: the diary writer lived through the flood.

exercises.prompt: Which words often show a firsthand account?
exercises.explain: The writer tells what happened to them: I and we.

exercises.prompt: An encyclopedia page about the flood is…
exercises.explain: The writer gathered facts from others: secondhand.

exercises.prompt: Two texts on the same topic are always built the same way.
exercises.explain: No: they can be built in different ways.

exercises.prompt: Text A: the rocket launched, then reached orbit, then landed. Text B: the landing worked because of new computers. How do they differ?
choices: A is time order; B is cause and effect.
exercises.explain: Text A tells steps in order; Text B explains a cause.

exercises.prompt: What might a firsthand account of a storm include?
exercises.explain: A firsthand account can share the writer's feelings.

exercises.prompt: What might a secondhand account give more of?
exercises.explain: Secondhand accounts often give more facts and the bigger picture.

exercises.prompt: A letter from a sailor on the ship is a firsthand account of the voyage.
exercises.explain: Yes: the sailor was on the voyage.

exercises.prompt: A reporter who arrived after a fire writes an article from interviews. The article is…
exercises.hint: Did the reporter see the fire?
exercises.explain: The reporter heard about it from others: secondhand.

exercises.prompt: Why read two accounts of the same event?
choices: To get a fuller, fairer picture.
To read the same words twice.
exercises.explain: Together they give feelings and facts: a fuller picture.

exercises.prompt: Text A compares frogs and toads. Text B tells a frog's life cycle in order. Which is true?
choices: A compares; B uses time order.
exercises.explain: A compares two animals; B tells steps in order.

exercises.prompt: "I watched the rocket shake the ground, and my heart raced." What kind of account is this?
exercises.explain: The writer was there and shares feelings: firsthand.

exercises.prompt: A secondhand account can't be trusted at all.
exercises.explain: No: it can be very accurate. It just gives a different view from someone who was there.

exercises.prompt: Which account would best explain why a bridge fell, with measurements?
exercises.hint: Which one gives facts and reasons?
exercises.explain: An engineer's report gives the facts and the causes.

exercises.prompt: Sort the texts: firsthand or secondhand account?
items: a diary written during a storm
a sailor's letter from the ship
exercises.hint: Was the writer there when it happened?
exercises.explain: The diary, the sailor's letter and your own photo come from someone who was there: firsthand. The encyclopedia and the reporter's article gather facts from others: secondhand.

exercises.prompt: Match each signal word to the structure it shows.
exercises.hint: Which words tell steps, reasons, comparisons or a problem?
exercises.explain: First, then, finally: time order. Because, so: cause and effect. Alike, different: compare and contrast. The problem is: problem and solution.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences by the structure their signal words show.
items: Frogs and toads are alike in many ways.
The ice melted, so the river rose.
Unlike toads, frogs have smooth skin.
exercises.hint: Look for signal words: first or then; because or so; alike or unlike.
exercises.explain: Time order: first, then. Cause and effect: because, so. Compare: alike, unlike. The signal words show how each text is built.

exercises.prompt: Sort what each account of a flood would most likely tell.
exercises.hint: A firsthand account gives feelings and close details; a secondhand one gathers facts and the big picture.
exercises.explain: The diary writer was there: the cold water, the fear at night, the smell of mud. The report gathers facts from many places: how many towns flooded, and the river's height.

exercises.prompt: Text A tells the Moon landing in time order. Put its events in order.
items: The astronauts walked on the Moon.
The spacecraft reached the Moon's orbit.
exercises.hint: A time-order text starts at the beginning: what had to happen first?
exercises.explain: The rocket launched, the spacecraft reached the Moon's orbit, the lander touched down, and then the astronauts walked on the Moon: the 1969 landing in time order.

exercises.prompt: Match each writer to the account they could write about the Moon landing.
items: a girl who watched it on TV
exercises.hint: Ask who was there, and what exactly each one saw.
exercises.explain: The astronaut was on the Moon: a firsthand account of the walk. The girl saw it on TV: a firsthand account of watching it. The history book gathers facts later: secondhand.

exercises.prompt: Which structure fits each topic best?
exercises.hint: Does the topic tell steps or events, explain why, or put two things side by side?
exercises.explain: Steps and events need time order: baking bread, a day at the fair. Why questions need cause and effect: the bridge, autumn leaves. Two things side by side need compare: cats and dogs, the Moon and Mars.
